extracted.intended_audience: Authors submitting manuscripts to F1000Research who may suggest peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on identifying and suggesting appropriate expert reviewers for articles submitted to F1000Research under its open, post-publication peer review model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identity transparency (NISO standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research uses NISO standard terminology: identities of reviewers are visible and review information is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key aspects: identity transparency (all identities visible); reviewer interacts with editor, other reviewers, and authors; review information published (review reports, submitted manuscript, reviewer identities); post-publication commenting is open. This sets expectations that reviewers will be identified and reports made public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial team manages reviewer identification and invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial team identifies and invites appropriate expert reviewers for each submission, managing the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may suggest reviewers but the editorial team checks that suggested reviewers meet criteria before inviting. The editorial team may also suggest reviewers to ensure balance or speed. Authors should not approach reviewers directly because this can influence and invalidate reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified (minimum credentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should typically hold a doctorate (PhD/MD/MBBS or equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions allowed in disciplines where doctorates are not typical (e.g., Education, Library Science) or where the individual has a demonstrable public record of expertise. If a suggested reviewer is rejected for lack of qualifications, editors may invite their Principal Investigator/Supervisor and consider the original person as a co-reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert (track record of relevant publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should have published at least three articles as lead author in a relevant topic, with at least one article published in the last five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a field does not typically measure expertise by publication record, or if suitability is demonstrable by other means, authors should provide an explanation of suitability. Authors must use judgement when approving automatically suggested reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality / conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be impartial and should not have competing interests that could bias their assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples of conflicts: having co-authored with any of the lead authors in the three years preceding publication of Version 1; having co-authored with any of the lead authors since publication of Version 1; currently working at the same institution as the authors; being a close collaborator with an author. In small/specialised fields where non-conflicted reviewers are impractical, authors should contact the Editorial Team to discuss options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global and institutional diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers for a given article must be from different institutions and a geographically-diverse set is strongly encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: large multi-site institutions (e.g., Max-Planck Institutes, University of California) are treated differently. If multiple suggestions come from the same country, the editorial team can invite only one at a time. Providing geographically-diverse reviewers helps avoid delays and provides international perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics expertise for complex analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: For studies with complex statistical analysis or new statistical methods, at least one suggested initial reviewer should have a proven track record as a statistics expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware the editors may request additional statistics experts as the peer review process progresses; include such experts in your suggested list where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of automated Reviewer Finder Tool (and author vetting)
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research provides a Reviewer Finder algorithm that scans the submission and reference list to suggest potential reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can suggest reviewers from this automatically generated ranked list (via 'Suggest Reviewers' in My Research), but must use their own judgement to verify that suggested reviewers have appropriate expertise. The tool is a convenience; authors remain responsible for ensuring suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methods for identifying reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended methods authors can use to find appropriate reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions include: use authors of references cited in your article; search databases such as Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for recent articles with relevant keywords; search prominent labs' websites for potential reviewers or their postdocs; use tools like the Journal/Author Name Estimator. Note that some databases (Web of Science, Scopus) are subscription-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dos when suggesting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive guidance authors should follow when providing reviewer suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do ensure suggested reviewers are experts in the relevant subject area; try to ensure a global spread and that reviewers come from separate institutions; ensure reviewers from the algorithm are suitable before approving them; discuss suggestions with co-authors (only the submitting author may enter suggestions unless changed by editorial staff); contact the editorial team if you have questions or if a suggested reviewer was rejected and you believe they are suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don'ts when suggesting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions authors must avoid when suggesting reviewers to preserve fairness and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't suggest reviewers who have recently closely collaborated with you or your co-authors (potential conflict of interest). Don't suggest reviewers who lack the right expertise — the editorial team will not invite them and doing so wastes time. Don't contact reviewers directly about the peer review process (this can influence or invalidate reviews); evidence of coercion will be investigated and may lead to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting-author procedural note
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the submitting author is able to provide reviewer suggestions via the submission system by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If co-authors would like to suggest reviewers, discuss this with the submitting author; the editorial team can change the submitting author on request so a co-author can provide suggestions directly.
